recent_developments: Q1 2026: Office vacancy reached 18.6%, down from 19.6% peak in Q1 2025; downtown prime vacancy dropped 1.5 points while suburban prime fell only 0.5 points (CBRE, March 2026).

January 2026: Commercial office loan delinquencies hit a record 12.34%, surpassing 2008 financial crisis levels; approximately $875 billion in commercial mortgages maturing in 2026 at rates 1.5–2% above original underwriting (Deloitte/PWC).

Q4 2025: Industrial leasing hit 940 million square feet for the year, up 12% from 2024; e-commerce accounted for 25% of warehouse absorption, up from 20% in 2024; AI tenants and data centers now a significant new tenant class (CBRE, January 2026).

Q2 2025: Retail leasing volume collapsed to 31.7 million square feet, down 29% year-over-year and the lowest quarterly total since at least 2000; new retail space deliveries fell to 6.98 million square feet, the lowest quarterly delivery on record (CoStar, Q2 2025).

2025: Demolitions and adaptive reuse conversions exceeded new commercial construction for the first time since 1988, with developers delivering only 281 million sq ft of industrial space, down 35% from 2024 (CBRE/Prologis, year-end 2025).

H1 2025: Commercial real estate M&A deal count collapsed from 3,286 to 846 transactions globally, though average deal size doubled to $255 million, signaling selective mega-deals by well-capitalized players (Deloitte M&A Review, June 2025).
themes: Bifurcation: prime assets vs. secondary distress
AI datacenters as new tenant class
Mortgage rate shock and maturity wall
how_it_makes_money: Commercial landlords generate revenue through annual rent payments (the largest revenue line), property sales, management fees, and triple-net leases (where tenants cover taxes, insurance, maintenance). Revenue depends entirely on occupancy rates and rental rates, which move with economic cycles, interest rates, and industry-specific trends (e.g., retail decline). Profit margins are high (45–46% in 2022, declining to ~40–42% by 2026 due to delinquencies and concessions) but heavily leveraged—operators finance 60–70% of property cost with debt, so interest rate spikes crush returns.
cost_structure: High capital intensity with 60–75% debt-to-asset ratio typical; operating expenses include property taxes (often the largest single cost in urban markets), insurance, maintenance, utilities, and property management (3–5% of rent). Financing costs are the largest variable; a 100-basis-point interest rate rise can cut NOI by 15–25% on levered deals. Newer properties have high depreciation expenses (tax deduction); older buildings face higher capex needs and rising conversion/demolition costs.
outlook: The 2026–2027 outlook is survival-focused for most operators. Interest rate stability (not cuts) at 5.5–6.5% will help resolve the maturity wall of $875 billion in 2026 loans, but refinancings will reset rates 1–2% higher than pre-2022 originations, forcing rent increases or equity injections. Delinquency rates peaked around 12% and may stabilize by 2027. Prime urban office will stabilize and potentially recover modestly, but secondary and tertiary markets face 5–10 years of rent pressure and vacancy (forecasters see normalization by 2027–2028). Industrial leasing will remain the growth engine, driven by e-commerce (pushing to 25% of retail by 2026) and data centers (capex-heavy, long-term leases). Retail will see continued fleet optimization—no new boom, but smaller leases (3,000–4,000 sq ft) to value-oriented tenants. Companies will demand shorter leases, flex space, and more concessions, squeezing landlord margins further. Consolidation will accelerate as small operators fail or sell to institutional buyers; only well-capitalized REITs with prime assets will generate returns >6% net of new borrowing costs.

title: US Commercial Shelving Manufacturing: 2025–2026 Industry Brief
one_liner: A bifurcated industry: warehouse racking surges on e-commerce and automation demand while retail shelving erodes amid store closures and shifting customer behavior.
overview: The US commercial shelving manufacturing industry is at a crossroads in 2025–2026. Warehouse and logistics shelving demand is accelerating rapidly, driven by booming e-commerce fulfillment networks, last-mile delivery expansion, and the adoption of AI-powered automated storage systems. Meanwhile, retail shelving faces persistent headwinds. Fifteen thousand brick-and-mortar store closures are expected in 2025 alone (more than double the 7,325 closures in 2024), with major chains like Macy's, Walgreens, and CVS shuttering locations. Tariffs on steel and imported components (ranging up to 25% from China in 2025) have squeezed margins, forcing manufacturers to absorb costs or pass them to end customers. Employment across the sector remains tight despite consolidation, with skilled labor shortages limiting production capacity.

key_stats.market_size: USD 11.8 billion (2026, warehouse racking segment); USD 6.3 billion (2026, retail shelving segment)
key_stats.growth: Warehouse racking: +3.14% YoY (2025–2026); retail shelving: +1.26% CAGR (2026–2034)
key_stats.employees: Approximately 20,500+ (declining due to automation, wage pressure from tariffs limiting hiring)
key_stats.businesses: Estimated 550–600 companies; consolidation accelerating as larger players absorb niche specialists
key_stats.profit_margin: Low single-digit margins (2–3% estimated 2025), constrained by tariffs and raw material inflation
key_stats.concentration: Moderate; Metro, Spacesaver, Interlake Mecalux, Lozier, and Madix lead; regional players compete fiercely on price

current_dynamics: Tariffs on Chinese steel and imported components hit 25% in 2025, creating cost cascades that manufacturers cannot always pass to price-sensitive retail customers, eroding profitability. Retail shelving demand is structurally declining as e-commerce captures market share and store closures accelerate (15,000 expected in 2025 vs. 7,325 in 2024), directly cutting demand from department stores and specialty retailers. Warehouse shelving is booming: 180,000+ warehouses now exist, averaging 181,370 sq ft, and over 210 million square meters of new space will be needed by 2035 to handle e-commerce volumes. Labor shortages persist (409,000+ unfilled manufacturing roles as of mid-2025) and wage pressures are rising, making domestic production more expensive. AI integration is reshaping the competitive landscape: smart racking systems with IoT sensors and automated retrieval systems (AS/RS) now command 35–50% adoption rates among logistics-focused customers, while traditional vendors lag.
one_sentence: Two sectors of one industry are diverging sharply in 2025–2026: warehouse storage thrives on automation and e-commerce expansion, while retail shelving withers under store closures and tariff pressure.
whats_growing: Warehouse racking and pallet storage systems (+3–5.6% CAGR through 2034), driven by e-commerce fulfillment sprawl and third-party logistics growth. Automated storage and retrieval systems (AS/RS) and AI-integrated shelving solutions are exploding: the AS/RS market alone was USD 10 billion in 2025 and is forecast to reach USD 15 billion by 2030. Mobile and modular racking designs are gaining share. Regional reshoring and nearshoring are opening new opportunities in North America for heavy-duty industrial shelving in manufacturing plants and distribution hubs.
whats_shrinking: Retail shop and gondola shelving demand is contracting as 15,000 brick-and-mortar stores close in 2025 (projected; major retailers include Macy's, Walgreens, CVS, and others). Traditional wire shelving and static systems are losing to smart and modular alternatives. Small and regional shelving manufacturers are exiting or consolidating; industry establishment count has fallen from ~569 in 2021 to an estimated 550–600 in 2026. Profit margins are compressing as tariffs raise input costs faster than manufacturers can raise prices.

outlook: The industry will remain polarized through 2027. Warehouse shelving is poised for sustained 4–5.6% annual growth, fueled by e-commerce expansion (over 210 million square meters of new warehousing needed by 2035) and the proliferation of AI-powered sorting and retrieval systems. Companies investing in automation and software integration will gain market share. Retail shelving will face continued headwinds: store closures are expected to accelerate further in 2026, holding growth to low single digits (1–2% CAGR). Tariff uncertainty remains a major threat; any new tariff escalations could further compress margins. Consolidation will accelerate as smaller players struggle to absorb tariff costs and invest in automation. Labor shortages will persist, limiting capacity growth for pure-play manufacturers unless wages rise significantly or reshoring policies create new opportunities. Smart, modular, and mobile systems will displace traditional static shelving. Manufacturers who diversify into logistics software (like Interlake Mecalux's intralogistics plays) or specialize in high-growth segments (automated systems, mobile racking) will outperform commodity players.
cost_structure: Raw materials (steel, aluminum, engineered wood) represent 40–50% of COGS; tariffs add 10–25% to imported input costs. Labor (assembly, fabrication, logistics) is 20–25% of COGS, with wage pressure rising due to shortages. Manufacturing overhead (plant, equipment, utilities) accounts for 15–20%. Distribution and logistics costs are 8–12%. Tariff-driven inflation is forcing cost absorption or price increases; manufacturers report 5% annual shelving cost inflation (as of 2025–2026). Profit margins compress to 2–3% in retail-focused segments; warehouse/logistics-focused producers achieve 3–5% due to higher customization and automation premiums.
how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from three streams: (1) Retail shelf fixtures and gondola units sold to department stores, grocery chains, and specialty retailers (37–44% of revenue historically, now declining). (2) Heavy-duty warehouse racking, pallet storage, and cantilever systems sold to 3PLs, fulfillment centers, and industrial manufacturers (44–50% of revenue, now growing). (3) Customization, mobile systems, lockers, and partitions (12–18% of revenue). Manufacturers compete on price, lead time, and customization. Margin is derived from production efficiency, material cost management, and scale economies. High-value segments (automation-integrated systems, smart shelving software bundles) command 15–25% premiums. Export revenue (to Canada, Mexico, UK) represents ~15% of sales but is pressured by tariffs and currency fluctuations. Service and maintenance contracts (installation, repairs, software) are growing as warehouses adopt more complex automated systems.

title: US Commercial Washing Machine Manufacturing
one_liner: A mature, capital-efficient industry serving laundromats and multifamily housing that is shrinking due to vacancies and import pressure, but gaining margin from technology adoption and labor substitution.
overview: The US commercial washing machine manufacturing industry remains small and highly concentrated, with 2026 revenue at $527.2 million after declining 4.2% in 2025. Demand is split between multifamily housing (39%), laundromats (28%), and on-premise facilities (hotels, hospitals). The core problem: rental vacancy rates surged to 7.3% nationally in Q2 2026—the highest since 2017—and construction is slowing, reducing replacement demand. Offsetting this decline are three tailwinds: technology adoption (IoT, smart cycles, digital payment systems), labor substitution (shortages making automation attractive), and regulatory cost recovery (water/energy efficiency premiums).

key_stats.profit_margin: 6.2% (2022), expected to edge up as consolidation continues
key_stats.concentration: Top 3 operators control ~61% of revenue; Whirlpool alone ~29% (2022 figures)

current_dynamics: The industry is trapped between structural headwinds and margin-creating technology. On demand: multifamily housing vacancy jumped from 6.8% (2024) to 7.3% (Q2 2026), eroding replacement cycles; Texas hit 13.3% vacancy. Laundromat demand is flat to declining as on-premise laundry competes. On supply: labor shortages (70% of commercial laundries affected per market research) are driving capex for automation—IoT monitoring, smart load sensing, predictive maintenance. Electrolux (39% of imports in 2022) competes hard; Alliance Laundry Systems, Girbau, and Dexter Laundry are consolidating. Tariffs on steel and aluminum (50%+ by mid-2025) add cost pressure but create preference for domestic makers. Energy regulations shifted in May 2025 (DOE rescinded amended water standards), easing compliance cost but reducing premium capture. The market is bifurcating: tech-enabled, card-payment locations command higher multiples in M&A; coin-only stores are stranded.
one_sentence: Commercial washing machine manufacturing is a low-growth, consolidating industry facing stagnant multifamily demand but gaining margin from labor-driven automation and regulatory compliance retrofits.

Rental vacancy rates remain a headwind; only if they rebalance below 7% (no consensus on timing) will multifamily replacement demand rebound. Exports face currency headwinds and import competition. Regulatory ease (DOE standard rollback) reduces retrofit premiums but removes a cost floor on competition.

title: US Communication Equipment Manufacturing
one_liner: A mature, consolidating industry pivoting from commodity phones and antennas toward high-margin 5G infrastructure while fighting tariffs and supply-chain relocation pressures.
overview: The US communication equipment manufacturing industry generates $36.8 billion (2026) and grew 3.4% annually from 2021–2026, driven primarily by nationwide 5G rollouts and massive MIMO antenna deployment. However, the sector remains undersized relative to overseas competitors; imports (especially from Vietnam, which now exceeds China) comprise 87% of domestic demand. Tariff reshuffles in 2025–2026 are redirecting supply chains away from China toward Vietnam and India, but US onshoring remains limited by labor costs and workforce shortages. The number of manufacturers continues to decline (568 businesses, down 0.5% annually), signaling ongoing consolidation among the remaining players who compete on R&D and proprietary tech rather than price.

key_stats.concentration: Medium; top players include L3Harris Technologies, Garmin, Amphenol, Broadcom; imports 87% of domestic demand
key_stats.profit_margin: 4.3% (2022); expected to stagnate as prices compress

current_dynamics: 5G infrastructure remains the defining growth engine: network operators are deploying massive MIMO antennas and cloud-native cores at scale, spurring demand for radio access network equipment and coherent optical transport systems. The tariff shock of early 2025 (145% on Chinese electronics) has shattered the old supply baseline: China's share of US cell phone imports collapsed from 81% (2024) to 45% (2025), while Vietnam now leads imports and Foxconn is expanding factories in Southeast Asia. Workforce constraints threaten expansion—the industry faces a 157,000-person shortfall by 2030 as fabs and factories struggle to hire workers with digital, robotics, and AI skills. AI chip competition is permanently siphoning semiconductor capacity away from communication equipment. Broadcom is building 5G RF filters in Fort Collins on Apple contracts; Qualcomm secured $7.86 billion in CHIPS Act funding but chip output remains capacity-constrained. Domestic demand remains robust ($123 billion broadly defined, 2025), but most units still come from overseas.
one_sentence: The industry trades lightweight consumer phones for sticky 5G infrastructure, but tariffs, chip shortages, and supply-chain shifts are remaking the map.
recent_developments: March 2025: Ericsson celebrates five years of continuous 24/7 5G equipment manufacturing at Lewisville, Texas facility
Early 2025: Trump administration imposes 145% tariff on Chinese electronics, collapsing China's share of US cell phone imports from 81% to 45% within months
March 2025: Forbes reports China no longer dominates US cell phone imports after two decades; Vietnam snaps China's 24-year streak
2025: Broadcom expands 5G FBAR filter manufacturing in Fort Collins, Colorado under multi-billion-dollar Apple deal
2025: CommScope divests DAS/wireless networks business to Amphenol; Era platform becomes benchmark for all-digital Distributed Antenna Systems
August 2025: Qualcomm launches Dragonwing Q-6690 processor with integrated 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0; Qualcomm revenue hits $44.3 billion (up 14% from 2024)
how_it_makes_money: Revenue splits three ways: (1) high-volume wireless infrastructure sold to telecom carriers (37%+ share of 5G RAN equipment market in 2025, growing toward cloud-native cores at 31% CAGR); (2) mobile phones and consumer devices (declining as manufacturing moves offshore, but Apple and emerging India production create pockets of demand); (3) satellite, GPS, and broadcast equipment (niche, stable). Gross margins compress on commodity items but expand on proprietary 5G silicon (Qualcomm, Broadcom) and antenna arrays. Business model shifting from volume to specialization: companies that can command premium pricing on advanced tech thrive; those stuck in low-end antennas and passive components struggle against cheap imports.
whats_growing: 5G infrastructure: RAN equipment, MIMO antennas, cloud-native network cores, coherent optical transport, and Open RAN architectures. Industrial IoT and smart-city deployments driving secondary demand. High-margin specialized silicon (5G chipsets, RF filters) growing faster than commodity goods. India manufacturing gaining traction as Apple shifts iPhone production there by end-2026 to avoid China tariffs. Publicly funded onshore capacity (Ericsson Texas, Broadcom Colorado, Qualcomm CHIPS Act plants) expanding, though still tiny relative to Asian output.
whats_shrinking: Low-end antenna manufacturing and passive components (losing ground to Vietnam/Bangladesh suppliers). Smartphone assembly (offshoring accelerates; Motorola had no US plants by 2014). Cable TV broadcasting equipment (TV subscriptions declining). Standalone GPS devices (replaced by phone navigation). Export revenue declining due to strong dollar and supply-chain shifts—exports fell from 64% of revenue (2017) to 38% (2022). Domestic manufacturer count declining: 634 companies (2022) → 574 by 2025, -1.6% annually. Profit margin stagnant despite revenue growth.
outlook: The industry will likely shrink 0.7% annually through 2031 as commodity products offload further to Asia and 5G maturation slows telecom capex cycles. However, pockets of growth will persist: (1) Industrial IoT and smart-factory buildouts will sustain antenna and sensor demand; (2) US onshoring efforts (tariff-driven, not competitiveness-driven) will keep select plants open in Texas, Colorado, Arizona but will not restore volume manufacturing; (3) AI-driven network optimization and edge compute will create new firmware and chipset needs. Tariff reshuffles (2025–2026) will cement Vietnam as the primary Asian hub, accelerating the exit of China-dependent players. Profit margins will remain compressed unless companies successfully pivot to proprietary software-defined networking stacks. Workforce constraints will limit expansion—the 157,000-worker gap by 2030 is real and unaddressed. M&A will accelerate: smaller independent antenna and RF shops will consolidate into tier-1 suppliers (L3Harris, Amphenol, CommScope ecosystem). The "true" US manufacturing base will contract to R&D centers, high-precision RF/antenna fabs, and 5G-specific nodes, while labor-intensive assembly remains in Southeast Asia.

High-margin specialized tech vs. commodity price collapse

title: Community Food Services in the US
one_liner: A nonprofit-dominated network of food banks, soup kitchens and pantries that serves 50 million food-insecure Americans, under strain from surging demand, rising food costs, volunteer shortages and volatile funding.
overview: The US Community Food Services industry is valued at $21.7 billion in 2026, down from pandemic-era peaks but stable since 2022. The sector serves nearly 50 million food-insecure Americans through 7,859 establishments including food banks, soup kitchens and pantries. Despite record-breaking 2025 fundraising (crisis-driven), the industry faces a structural funding squeeze: shrinking corporate donations of leftover food, volunteer fatigue from 75% of pantries having zero paid staff, and a $32 billion national food budget shortfall that means vulnerable households face a weekly gap averaging $22.37 per person. Regional hunger is accelerating—Texas now shows 19.4% food insecurity (up from 17.6% prior year), and Massachusetts reached 40% in 2025—while tariffs and inventory efficiency at retailers are reducing traditional donation streams.

key_stats.employees: Approximately 59,000-68,000 (mix of paid and volunteer staff)
key_stats.concentration: Fragmented: low consolidation, nonprofit-dominated, Feeding America is largest player
key_stats.profit_margin: 4.9-5.9% (low; most nonprofit operators spend nearly all revenue on services)

current_dynamics: Hunger is no longer pandemic-driven but structural. Food insecurity reached 47.9 million people in 2024 and is rising again in 2025-2026, with 1 in 7 households (13.7%) experiencing it and 1 in 4 children in Texas facing hunger. The sector's operating model is breaking: demand is outpacing food bank capacity, yet donations of manufactured goods are shrinking because retailers now manage inventory more efficiently. Corporate giving rose 3.1% nominally in 2025 but flatlined when adjusted for inflation. Most critical—volunteer fatigue is real: 75% of Maine's 600 hunger agencies have zero paid staff, and All Faiths Food Bank in Florida needs 800 volunteers for a summer season. Regional federal funding cuts (California facing $50+ million state budget cuts) collide with new policy headwinds: SNAP nutrition education funding eliminated in FY2026, junk-food bans in 18 states, and 25% of administrative costs now shifted to states starting FY2027. Tariff-driven food price increases (beef +9.4%, dairy and produce inflation mid-2026) are widening the gap between what food banks can source and what families need.
one_sentence: Nonprofit food banks and pantries serving 50 million Americans face a "perfect storm" of surging hunger, shrinking donation supplies, volunteer shortages, and policy funding cuts that have eroded the pandemic-era relief cushion.
whats_growing: Food insecurity: 47.9 million people in 2024 (up from 37.2 million pre-pandemic), with fastest growth among children, working-age poor, and non-White households. Demand for food bank services is at historic highs. Charitable fundraising surged in 2025 ($1+ billion raised by food banks year-end from crisis donations and first-time givers), though retention is fragile. Emergency federal food assistance (TEFAP funding ~$2.2 billion FY2024 plus $500M CCC allocation FY2025) has held steady. Regional networks and technology adoption are expanding (NYC's PantryLink initiative seeking tech-enabled solutions to improve dignity, nutrition, and efficiency).
whats_shrinking: Traditional corporate and grocery donations: manufacturers and retailers now use advanced inventory management, reducing surplus goods. Private retail donations from grocery stores are down. Volunteer availability, especially among seniors (many avoiding in-person work post-pandemic). Government state-level support: California's food banks facing $50+ million in state funding cuts. SNAP education programs: mandatory nutrition education funding eliminated in FY2026. Pandemic-era facility expansion: San Francisco-Marin Food Bank shuttered pop-up pantries in 2025 as federal/state/local emergency funding ended. For-profit food company stability: farm bankruptcies jumped 46% in 2025 (315 filings, up 70% in Midwest), reducing supply chain resilience.

outlook: The industry faces a decade-long contraction. The USDA's decision to stop collecting food security data after 2026 marks the end of a 40-year benchmark, leaving future hunger tracking to Feeding America and nonprofits. Mid-2026 is a critical inflection point: tariffs will begin hitting grocery shelves, food bank operating costs are up 25% since 2023, and the traditional donation model (retail surplus) has permanently shrunk. Policy headwinds accelerate: SNAP eligibility tightens, states absorb more admin costs, and 18 states are blocking less-nutritious SNAP purchases. Volunteer-dependent infrastructure will likely consolidate or close in regions with declining donation streams (expect more shutdowns like San Francisco's pop-up pantries). Tech adoption (digital ordering, nutritional intelligence, micro-delivery) will accelerate among larger networks but leave rural and small operators further behind. Without major federal intervention or a shift in corporate donations, food banks will continue rationing services and deferring facility upgrades. The industry will likely remain around $21-22 billion through 2027, neither growing nor shrinking significantly, but delivering fewer meals per person served as costs rise and budgets flatten.

title: US Community Housing & Homeless Shelters Industry
one_liner: A nonprofit-dominated safety net providing emergency shelter and permanent housing for the homeless, now strained by record homelessness, federal policy whiplash, and the affordability crisis.
overview: The US Community Housing and Homeless Shelters industry operates almost entirely through nonprofits (97.6% of establishments) and remains almost entirely dependent on federal, state, and local government funding. In 2025, the industry reached $22.3 billion in revenue and contracted 0.8% in 2026 to $22.2 billion, reflecting uncertainty over HUD policy and funding volatility. The underlying problem has worsened dramatically: homelessness hit an all-time high of 771,480 people in January 2024 (18% jump from 2023), though preliminary 2025 data showed a modest 2% decline to approximately 745,000 people. The fundamental driver is the housing affordability crisis: 22.7 million renter households were cost-burdened in 2024, spending more than 30% of income on rent, while asking rents remain elevated despite a softer 2026 market. Federal funding for homeless assistance increased to $4.4 billion for FY 2026, but HUD faced a 44% budget cut overall, creating chaos for shelter operators who cannot plan beyond the current year.

key_stats.profit_margin: 6.3% (2022); nearly all operators are nonprofits, so most generate zero operating profit
key_stats.concentration: Low — fragmented across many small nonprofits; no dominant players

current_dynamics: The industry faces a perfect storm. Homelessness reached all-time highs (771,480 in January 2024, up 34% from January 2014), yet 2025 showed a rare 2% decline to 745,000 — suggesting the trend may have peaked but remains catastrophically high. The root cause is unaffordable housing: 22.7 million renter households were cost-burdened in 2024, with 12.1 million paying more than 50% of income for rent. Housing nonprofits report 59% cannot meet current demand (2024 data), and 80% expect demand to rise further. Federal funding creates whiplash: HUD announced $4.4 billion in homeless assistance grants for FY 2026, yet the broader HUD budget faced a 44% cut. In November 2025, HUD attempted to slash Permanent Supportive Housing (PSH) funding from 90% to 30% of Continuum of Care grants, threatening 170,000 existing residents, but a court order in January 2026 forced HUD to reverse course and reinstate the original funding rules. Staff shortages plague shelters: 44% of nonprofits reported vacancies in 2025, and 55% cannot offer competitive salaries to compete with private/public sectors. Housing affordability in coastal metros remains dire (Seattle rents at $2,238/month in 2025), while rural and suburban PSH programs face elimination risk. The Housing First model continues to show strong outcomes (62% housing retention after two years vs. 31% in treatment-as-usual), yet underfunding prevents scale.
one_sentence: A $22.2 billion nonprofit safety net confronting record homelessness driven by unaffordable housing, federal funding volatility, and insufficient capacity to meet surging demand.
how_it_makes_money: Nearly all revenue comes from federal (HUD), state, and local government grants and contracts; nonprofits also rely on private donations and foundation grants. HUD's Continuum of Care program funds permanent supportive housing, transitional housing, and emergency shelters. Permanent Supportive Housing accounts for 39.2% of industry beds and receives the largest share of funding. Temporary and emergency shelters (32% of beds) serve victims of domestic violence, runaway youth, and families in crisis and draw funding from HUD, Department of Health and Human Services, and Department of Veterans Affairs. Rental assistance for low-income families accounts for nearly 80% of HUD's $4.4 billion homeless assistance budget (2026). For-profit operators are rare; nearly all organizations are nonprofits that break even or operate at thin margins.
cost_structure: Labor is the dominant cost for shelters (staff for 24-hour operations, case managers, counselors). Facility costs (rent or mortgages for buildings, utilities, maintenance) are significant. Food and supplies for residents represent ongoing operating expenses. Technology for intake, case management, and reporting (HMIS systems) is increasingly mandatory for federal funding compliance. Most nonprofits operate on razor-thin margins (6.3% profit in 2022, but mostly in for-profit minority), meaning wage growth and facility upgrades are squeezed when funding stalls. Homelessness services organizations depend on government grants for 50%+ of revenue, making them uniquely vulnerable to budget cuts.
whats_growing: Permanent Supportive Housing units are up 25% over the past decade to 400,000 nationwide, reflecting adoption of Housing First philosophy. Older adults age 55+ are the fastest-growing homeless demographic and now represent nearly 40% of PSH residents. Hotel-to-housing conversions are accelerating: post-pandemic hotel oversupply is being repurposed into affordable and supportive housing (e.g., Pierce County, WA converting 117-unit hotel to emergency shelter plus PSH, Denver converting hotels to affordable housing). Demand for digital case management and HMIS systems is surging as shelters move intake online and deploy real-time bed tracking. Veteran homelessness is declining (record low 32,495 in January 2025, down 56% from 2010), reflecting targeted VA programs and dedicated funding streams.
whats_shrinking: Overall revenue contracted 0.8% in 2026 due to federal funding uncertainty and attempted policy shifts. Temporary/emergency shelters face phase-outs in some states (Massachusetts phasing out hotel-based shelter FY 2025-2026). Hotel-based shelter models are losing favor as temporary solutions, with states shifting to permanent housing. Charitable giving to nonprofits has declined since the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act reduced tax incentives for donations. The nonprofit staff capacity is strained: while 79% of nonprofits maintained or grew staff in 2025, wage gaps with private/public sectors widen, making recruitment harder. Long-term funding visibility is shrinking due to year-to-year grant uncertainty.
major_players: Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) — federal funder and policy driver
Local housing authorities and city/county government agencies — direct operators and co-funders
Catholic Charities USA — large national nonprofit operator of homeless services
The Salvation Army — major nonprofit shelter operator nationwide
National Alliance to End Homelessness — policy and advocacy organization
Community Solutions — homeless services nonprofit
Local Community Development Corporations — operate housing and shelter programs regionally
recent_developments: January 2024: Homelessness hits all-time high of 771,480 people, up 18% year-over-year, driven by housing affordability collapse and expiration of pandemic eviction protections.

November 2025: HUD attempts drastic funding shift, limiting Continuum of Care funds for Permanent Supportive Housing to 30% (down from 90%), threatening 170,000 PSH residents; court blocks move in December 2025.
January 2026: HUD forced to reinstate original funding rules after judicial order; Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2026 includes measures protecting PSH and housing funding.
May 2026: HUD announces $3.5 billion in CoC Program renewal funding for nearly 6,000 projects expiring mid-2026.
2025: Preliminary Point-in-Time data shows homelessness declining 2% to approximately 745,000 people, suggesting potential peak in trend after years of increases.
2025-2026: Housing nonprofits report 59% cannot meet demand; 44% of nonprofits have staff vacancies; wage competition with private sector intensifies while federal funding remains volatile.
outlook: The industry faces a bifurcated future. Short-term (2026-2027): Homelessness may stabilize or continue gradual decline if housing affordability slightly improves and federal funding holds. However, HUD policy remains a wild card after the 2025 funding fight; another attempt to defund PSH would destabilize 400,000+ residents. Federal funding for homelessness assistance is expected to rise modestly, but HUD's broader 44% budget cut limits overall capacity. Nonprofits will continue to struggle with wage competitiveness and staff turnover (55% cite inability to pay competitive salaries). Housing First programs will expand (strong evidence of 62% retention rates) but remain underfunded relative to need. Medium-term (2027-2030): The housing affordability crisis is structural — supply is 2 million units short as of early 2025 — meaning homelessness will remain elevated without massive housing construction. Federal spending on social services is projected to increase 4.11% annually through 2028 (from 2022 baseline), which may sustain funding, but depends on political will and economic conditions. If recessions trigger job losses, homelessness will spike again. Technology adoption (digital intake, HMIS systems) will become standard, improving data quality and outcomes. Hotel-to-housing conversions will add inventory but at slow pace. Permanent Supportive Housing will remain the highest-impact model but faces ongoing debate about funding levels.

Nonprofit workforce burnout and wage compression
